text: The void-free blind microvia copper electroplating process is a key technology in HDI PCB manufacturing. This work systematically studied the influence of the Acid Blue 1 (AB1) leveler on blind microvia filling. AB1 exhibits excellent suppression during electroplating, with its efect strengthening as the AB1 concentration increases. Chronopotentiometry was used to study the interaction among AB1, SPS, and PEG. There is a synergistic suppressing interaction between the new leveler AB1 and suppressor PEG, while there is competition between AB1 and accelerator SPS. During electrodeposition, AB1 can adsorb on the copper substrate to reduce active sites and suppress copper electrodeposition, based on theoretical studies and in situ infrared spectroscopy. At the optimized electroplating process, void-free microvia filling is achieved with 20 mg/L AB1 and successive electroplating confirms the stability of AB1. Based on difusion diferences among additives and the competition between AB1 and SPS, a gradient competitive adsorption superfilling mechanism was proposed to illustrate the filling process of the AB1–SPS–PEG system. AB1 is beneficial to improving flatness and lowering surface roughness of the copper layer, which is conducive to reducing signal losses during high-frequency transmission. Additionally, AB1 can modulate the preferential formation of Cu(111) and Cu(200) and facilitate grain refinement.

text: High-density interconnect (HDI) printed circuit boards (PCBs) serve as a foundational platform for connecting all kinds of electronic components in electronic products, thus attracting significant research attention. 1 With the trend toward smallersized electronic devices with higher performance, stricter requirements are imposed on PCB design and manufacturing technology. 2,3 Especially in the fields of high-performance computing, high-speed communication, and precision instruments, the reliability and performance of PCBs are directly related to the performance and stability of the final products. Blind microvia filling is a key interconnect technology in the manufacturing process of PCBs, allowing for electrical connections between diferent layers in the circuit board. 4,5 The application of this technology enhances PCB design flexibility, enabling more complex circuit layouts and greater space utilization.

text: Copper is widely used as an interconnect line in blind microvias for PCB manufacturing due to its good electronic (thermal and electrical conductivity) and mechanical (wear resistance and elongation, etc.) properties. 6,7 The filling of blind microvias with copper is achieved through electroplating technology. 8–10 In PCBs, copper not only provides a stable electrical connection but also enhances the structural strength of HDI PCBs, improving heat and wear resistance. 11 Moreover, copper interconnect lines effectively reduce losses in signal transmission and enhance signal integrity, which is especially important for high-frequency and high-speed circuits. 12 During copper electroplating, it is essential to adjust the metal deposition process in local microvias to avoid the formation of void defects caused by the edge effect, which can undermine the properties of the copper interconnect layer. The most common method is the addition of proper additives. 13–15

text: The additives used in copper electroplating fall into three categories: accelerators, suppressors, and levelers. 16 The most commonly used accelerator, suppressor, and leveler is bis-(sodium sulfopropyl)- disulfide (SPS), polyethylene glycol (PEG), and Janus Green B (JGB). 17 During electroplating, density functional theory (DFT) calculations, in situ Raman spectroscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) studies reveal that the disulfide bond of SPS will break up, with the sulfurcontaining side adsorbing on the copper base, while the other side (containing a sulfonic acid group) captures free Cu ^ 2 + to accelerate reduction with adsorbed Cl - through the ‘‘bridging efect’’. 18–20 As for PEG, in situ Raman and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations confirm the formation of PEG-Cu^2+-Cl^- adsorbate complexes, which increase the energy barrier and suppress copper electrodeposition. 21–23 Mass spectrometry (MS) and DFT calculations demonstrate that the azo group of JGB competes with the reduction of Cu ^ 2 + to obtain electrons, leading to dissociation 24,25 into phenazine derivatives that can also adsorb on active sites to suppress copper growth. 26,27 Among these additives, levelers are key components for achieving defect-free filling in blind vias. 28 Nowadays, triphenylmethane derivatives are promising levelers and have been used in throughhole and blind-hole filling due to the unlocalized orbital distribution of the tertiary amine structure. 29,30

text: In this work, a novel triphenylmethane derivative, Acid Blue 1 (AB1), was selected as a potential leveler, and the efects of diferent concentrations of AB1 on copper electroplating were investigated. The interactions among three diferent types of additives were studied using galvanostatic measurements. The influencing mechanism of AB1 on the copper cathode surface during electroplating was also studied theoretically and experimentally. The filling performance of AB1 in blind microvias was examined, and the electroplating process was optimized. Additionally, the surface morphology and roughness of the copper interconnect layer were analyzed, and finite element simulation was employed to study the high-frequency signal transmission losses influenced by AB1, while phase structure was investigated by XRD.

text: 3.1.1 CV analysis. Cyclic voltammetry was used to examine AB1 during electroplating, 42 as shown in Fig. 1a and Fig. S1 (ESI†). The cathodic onset potential decreases as AB1 concentration increases (Fig. S1, ESI†). The onset potential without AB1 was about -430 mV, while it shifts negatively to -575 mV after adding 10 mg L^-1 AB1, indicating that AB1 efectively increases cathodic polarization. In addition, the onset potential decreases from -583 mV to - 6 5 0 mV with additive concentrations rising from 20 mg L^-1 to 150 mg L ^ - 1, demonstrating an intensified suppressing efect on copper electrodeposition with higher AB1 concentrations. The anodic stripping area also declines continuously with increasing AB1 concentration, suggesting a reduction in the amount of electrodeposited Cu during the cathodic process. We calculated the anodic stripping coulomb (ASC) values according to eqn (S1) for quantitative evaluation of AB1 (details in ESI†). 43 Fig. 1b shows that the ASC of VMS is 7 1.0 ~C~ dm ^ - 2, which decreases by 28% to 51.4 ~C~dm ^ - 2 with 10 mg ~L~ ^ - 1 AB1, indicating that trace AB1 (10 mg L ^ - 1) can significantly suppress copper electrodeposition. At 20 mg L^-1 and 30 mg L^-1 AB1 concentrations, the ASC is 4 7.8 ~C~ dm ^ - 2 and 42.7 ~C~dm ^ - 2,, both lower than 5 0 ~C~ dm ^ - 2.. The ASC further decreases to 35.8 ~C~dm ^ - 2 with AB1 concentration at 50 mg L^-1 Notably, the ASC drops to 2 5.8 ~C~ dm ^ - 2, accounting for 36% of VMS. Overall, cyclic voltammetry analysis indicates that AB1 suppresses copper electrodeposition.

text: 3.1.3 Chronopotentiometry analysis. It is important to study the interaction among SPS (accelerator), PEG (suppressor), and AB1 (leveler), as it provides a deeper understanding of the filling mechanism in microvias. 45 Traditionally, galvanostatic measurement is applied to study possible interactions by changing the injection order of the three types of additives. Fig. 1c (up) shows the change in cathodic potential after injecting additives into the testing solution. The cathodic potential declines (230 mV) after adding PEG, indicating its suppressing efect. Upon introducing AB1, the cathodic potential further decreases (31 mV), suggesting synergistic cooperation between AB1 and PEG. However, after the addition of SPS, the cathodic potential shifts positively (42 mV), indicating the accelerating efect of SPS in the presence of AB1 and PEG. By altering the additive injection order, SPS can cause a positive shift of 205 mV in cathodic potential after PEG injection, suggesting that SPS can replace PEG to accelerate copper electrodeposition, consistent with previous work. 46 Following AB1 injection, the cathodic potential changes negatively (-191 mV). Additionally, the potential reaches the same level regardless of injection order, further verifying the competition between SPS and AB1. Fig. 1c (down) provides a schematic diagram illustrating the relationships among SPS, PEG, and AB1, showing cooperation between AB1 and PEG, but competition between AB1 and SPS.

text: 3.2.1 Adsorption analysis. The influencing mechanism was studied using DFT calculations and in situ infrared spectroscopy. 47–49 The AB1 formula and its optimized structure are shown in Fig. S2 (ESI†). Fig. 2a shows the local electron affinity (LEA) distribution, with the blue color indicating high electrophilicity and red representing nucleophilicity. The -SO_3 area (high electrophilicity) in AB1 is conducive to forming interactions with the copper substrate due to vacant d orbitals. The adsorption equilibrium configuration of AB1 on the copper substrate is shown in Fig. 2b and Fig. S3 (ESI†), with color representations detailed in the ESI.† The quasi-plane structure of AB1 adsorbs nearly parallel to the copper substrate, with the -SO_3 functional group connected to the benzene ring of AB1 preferentially adsorbing on the substrate. Fig. 2c shows the 2D charge density difference of the adsorption configuration after equilibrium. The blue and red colors represent charge depletion and accumulation, demonstrating charge transfer between copper and AB1. It is believed that AB1 adsorbs on the cathode surface to reduce active sites and increase cathodic polarization.

text: 3.2.2 DOS analysis. Density of states (DOS) analysis provides insight into the interaction at the orbital level. 32 Fig. 2e shows the clear orbital overlap among the d orbitals of Cu, the s orbitals of N, and the p orbitals of O, indicating orbital interactions among the copper substrate, N atoms, and O atoms. In contrast, there is no orbital overlap between S and Cu, demonstrating that S atoms are not directly adsorbed on the copper substrate, consistent with the calculated adsorption configuration. To understand the specific orbital interactions in more detail, the PDOS (projected density of state) was calculated, as shown in Fig. 2f. Firstly, the pz orbitals of N atoms exhibit the largest overlap with the dyz and dz2 orbitals of Cu, while a strong hybridization occurs between py and pz orbitals of O atoms and dyz and dz2 orbitals of Cu. DOS analysis confirms significant d and p orbital hybridization among O, N, and Cu, further verifying the adsorption configuration and providing a deeper understanding of the adsorption mechanism. In summary, AB1 can adsorb on the copper cathode to reduce active sites and act as a barrier to suppress the reduction of free Cu ^ 2 +

text: 3.3.1 Electroplating performance. The optimization of the electroplating process is shown in Fig. 3, with the used devices illustrated in Fig. 3c. Without AB1, the growth rate at the opening area is higher than that at the bottom and side walls, leading to void defects in microvias with both diameters (125 mm and 150 mm). At an AB1 concentration of 10 mg L ^ - 1, the growth rate at the opening area decreases due to AB1 adsorption, which suppresses copper growth. However, this relatively low concentration is not conducive to establishing an efective concentration gradient, resulting in defects forming in the 125 mm microvias and concave growth in the 150 mm microvias. With 20 mg ~L~ ^ - 1 \ AB1, an efective concentration gradient is formed, allowing copper to grow from bottom to top without defects in either microvias. Besides, the compact and flat copper morphology from the top view in Fig. S4 (ESI†) indicates that AB1 improves copper quality compared to layers obtained without it. In contrast, the commonly used leveler Janus Green B (Fig. S5, ESI†) produces a copper layer that contains gas holes, despite yielding a flat and defect-free surface, demonstrating that AB1 is superior in enhancing copper quality. The influence of morphology will be discussed in Section 3.4.1. When the AB1 concentration increases further to 3 0 mgL ^ - 1, the excessive concentration weakens the concentration gradient, causing the bottom-up growth mode to shift to a conformal growth mode in the 150 mm microvias. Overall, 20 mg/L AB1 is determined to be optimum.

text: 3.3.2 Filling mechanism. The difusion property of AB1 was studied using molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, as shown in Fig. S8 (ESI†). Based on the Einstein equation (eqn (S2), ESI†), the difusion coeficient for AB1 $\left( D _ { \mathbf { A B 1 } } \right)$ is 2  $1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , which is close to the difusion coeficient for PEG $\left( D _ { \mathrm { P E G } } , 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } \right) ^ { 5 0 }$ and one order smaller than that for SPS $\big ( D _ { \mathrm { S P S } } , 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathrm { ~ m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { ~ s } ^ { - 1 } \big ) . ^ { 5 1 }$ This illustrates that the leveler AB1 and suppressor PEG have slower difusion transport compared to the accelerator SPS. Coupled with the interactions among the three additives discussed in Section 3.1.3, namely the competition between AB1 and SPS, as well as cooperation between AB1 and PEG, gradient competitive adsorption superfilling was proposed to illustrate the AB1–SPS–PEG system, with a schematic diagram shown in Fig. 3d. At the initial stage (3d1), different additives are distributed uniformly within the microvias. As the filling process progresses (3d2), a concentration gradient for the additives forms due to their consumption and local diffusion transport limitations within the microvias. However, the concentration ratio of SPS to PEG and AB1 at the bottom increases compared to that at the opening area due to the differing diffusion properties among the three additives; specifically, $D _ { \mathrm { S P S } }$ is significantly larger than $D _ { \mathbf { A B 1 } }$ and $D _ { \mathbf { P E G } } .$ . As a result, the growth rate at the bottom is improved by the increased accelerating effect from the relatively amount of SPS, while growth at the opening area is effectively suppressed since AB1’s mass transport is not limited due to convection, leading to copper growth from the bottom to the top. At the final stage (3d3), the three additives redistribute uniformly at the opening area, resulting in the same growth rate across different areas. No momentum plating phenomena occur in the AB1–SPS–PEG system. 52

text: 3.4.1 Efect of AB1 on morphology. Fig. 4 and 5a show the surface morphology of the copper layer observed by SEM and Olympus conformal laser microscope. 53 Small bump particles are present on the uneven copper surface electrodeposited without AB1. After introducing 10 mg $\mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ AB1, the surface flatness improves greatly, and the copper layer becomes compact, although large bump morphology remains. As the AB1 concentration continues to rise, the flatness of the copper layer further improves. Using the Olympus conformal laser microscope, the surface roughness $\left( R _ { \mathrm { z } } \right)$ was calculated, as shown in Fig. 5b. $R _ { \mathrm { z } }$ is 128 nm for the copper layer obtained without AB1 and decreases to 92 nm with 10 mg $\mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ AB1. Furthermore, $R _ { \mathrm { z } }$ values obtained from 20 mg $\mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ and 30 mg $\mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ are 83 nm and 75 nm, respectively. The above analysis indicates that AB1 has a micro-scale leveling efect.

text: 3.4.2 Efect of AB1 on signal loss. The influence of AB1 on signal loss during high-frequency transmission was studied using finite element simulation. 54 Fig. 5c shows that signal loss is influenced by surface roughness and applied frequency. Total loss increases with rising frequency and R _ z. Additionally, the total loss with frequency for the copper layer obtained with JGB is also calculated (Fig. S5d, ESI†). In comparison, the signal loss obtained with AB1 is smaller than with JGB at the same frequency due to a lower R _ z for AB1. The skin efect for the optimized copper layer with 20 mg L^-1 AB1 and without AB1 is shown in Fig. 5d and e. At a relatively low frequency (10 GHz), current density is distributed uniformly in the copper layer obtained from 2 0 mgL ^ - 1. Even at high frequency (100 GHz), the current density remains relatively well distributed. However, for the copper layer obtained without AB1, the current density mainly concentrates near the surface area at 10 GHz. Simulation results indicate that AB1 helps mitigate the influence of the skin efect during high-frequency signal transmission by improving surface flatness.

raw: 4. Conclusion

text: A novel leveler, Acid Blue 1, was used to achieve void-free copper filling in blind microvias. Electrochemical tests (CV and EIS) confirm the suppressive efect on the reduction of Cu ^ 2 +. During copper electroplating, there is a synergistic suppression between AB1 and PEG, but competition between AB1 and SPS. DFT calculations and in situ infrared spectroscopy provide a deeper understanding of AB1 adsorption configuration on the copper substrate during electrodeposition, indicating that AB1 can reduce active sites and act as a barrier adsorption layer to increase cathodic polarization. After electroplating optimization, microvias with diameters of 125 mm and 150 mm can be filled with 20 mg L^-1 AB1 at 1.5 Adm ^ - 2; the good stability of AB1 indicates its industrial potential. A gradient competitive adsorption superfilling mechanism was proposed to explain the filling process for the AB1–SPS–PEG system. The diffusion differences among the three additives and the competition between AB1 and SPS are key to achieving bottom-up growth in microvias. AB1 improves the copper layer quality, enhances surface flatness, refines the grains, and reduces signal losses during high-frequency transmission. Additionally, AB1 suppresses the formation of Cu(220) while promoting the formation of Cu(111) and Cu(200).
